segments.en: Mosi-oa-Tunya. It means the smoke that thunders, and once you hear it you'll understand why. A wide curtain of water drops from the Zambezi River into a deep gorge, and spray rises like smoke high above the trees.
Most visitors know it as Victoria Falls, shared between Zambia and Zimbabwe. In the dry season, brave swimmers even sit in a natural rock pool right at the edge of the falls, with a guide close by.
Zambia is a landlocked country in southern Africa, high on a plateau, so its climate is often milder than you might expect. The rains come in summer, turning the land a brilliant green.
Rivers shape life here. The Zambezi, the Kafue and the Luangwa wind through wild country, and in the South Luangwa valley, guides lead walking safaris past elephants, giraffes, hippos and leopards.
Each year, millions of fruit bats arrive at Kasanka to feast on wild fruit, filling the evening sky, one of the great wildlife gatherings of Africa.
Lusaka, the capital, is busy and growing, with bustling markets full of fabrics, carvings, fresh vegetables and dried fish from the lakes.
More than seventy peoples call Zambia home, and the country's motto is One Zambia, One Nation. English is the official language, and Bemba, Nyanja, Tonga and Lozi are widely spoken.

Greetings are gentle and unhurried. People often clap their hands softly when greeting, and a polite way to show respect is to hand something over with both hands, or with your left hand touching your right arm.

At almost every meal you'll find nshima, a thick, smooth porridge made from maize meal. You roll a small ball in your right hand and use it to scoop up relish, such as leafy greens, beans, fish or chicken.

Traditional ceremonies are grand and colourful. In the Kuomboka, the Lozi king travels by a huge royal barge from the flooded plains to higher ground, paddled by teams of rowers as drums echo across the water.
Other ceremonies celebrate the harvest, honour ancestors or welcome young people into adulthood, with singing, dancing and feasting that can last for days.
Football is the favourite sport, and Zambians still talk proudly of the day their national team, the Chipolopolo, the copper bullets, won the Africa Cup of Nations in 2012.
So listen once more to the thunder of the falls, then walk across the old bridge over the gorge, where Zimbabwe is waiting on the other side.
